Another In Our Series On . . . 


Why I Direct A Camp 

BRUNO MORAWETZ, 
Camp Ponacka. 


Between the editor’s request for this 
contribution and my present writing 
Camp Ponacka held its 15th Annual 
Reunion. To mark the occasion we 
held an Anniversary Banquet and in¬ 
vited all former staff and campers. 
This contact with the past placed by¬ 
gone events in a better perspective and 
provided me with many answers to the 
question “Why I am Happy to direct 
a camp”, but not “Why I direct a 
camp”. 

The two questions are really quite 
distinct. I started a camp because I 
like the out of doors, I value the fresh¬ 
ness and honesty of youth and I looked 
forward to many summers spent in 
that kind of environment. Once a 
camp is established, it starts to move 
the director. He realizes that January 
is the month for sending out folders 
and hence November the time for their 
preparation. The removal of each 
sheet on the calendar prompts him to 
do the next thing. In each of these 
activities there may be little awareness 
of why the camp is directed. I need 
not mention that financial obligations 
play their share in urging one on. 

It would be easy to say that I direct 
a camp because I am a passionate be¬ 
liever in the virtues of group experi¬ 
ence, the promotion of water safety, 
the teaching of camping skills, charac¬ 
ter building, etc. Of course I believe 
in these and I hope they will flourish, 
but it would be pretentious to give 
these as reasons for directing a camp. 


I will therefore revert to the ques¬ 
tion “Why I am happy to direct a 
camp”. I have always harboured the 
vague hope, often pierced with doubts, 
that some good will result from my 
activity. It pleased me to learn from 
my recent contact with former camp¬ 
ers that this hope was not entirely un¬ 
founded. One former camper wrote: 
“I wish I could come to the Anniver¬ 
sary Banquet but I shall be writing my 
final term examinations at the Semin¬ 
ary, for on May 26th his Eminence 
Cardinal Leger will ordain me a Priest 
of Jesus Christ”. After comparing the 
\ocations of priests and camp directors, 
each in his own way “showing the love 
of God in our fraternal love for one 
another”, he says, “This I learned from 
you, this I remember and this I try to 
practise to the best of my ability ...” 

Other campers used phrases like, 
“Fifteen years seems such a long time 
—especially when you get past twenty- 
five—yet I remember with fond mem¬ 
ories the good times which we enjoyed 
. . . and which remain with every 
camper for his lifetime”. 

It would be unnecessary to prolong 
these references, but they do serve to 
explain why I am happy to direct a 
camp. The influence exerted on mem¬ 
bers of the staff is often more gratify¬ 
ing. They are at the stage of decision, 
the choice of a career and a mate for 
life. They are in search of concrete 
solutions to the riddles of life and of 
their own existence and these oppor¬ 
tunities must not be overlooked. 


140 


Canadian Camping 



If I were asked to point to man’s 
most precious possession I would say 
without hesitation that it is the oppor¬ 
tunity to live creatively. Man is made 
in God’s image, but in what sense? In 
terms of goodness, power, wisdom he 
falls very short. But in as much as 
God is identified with the creative 
principle in the world, it is true to say 
that only man has the power to create. 
Few occupations afford a better oppor¬ 
tunity of being creative than that of 
the camp director. He breathes the 
soul into the fragments which go to 
make up a camp. In this atmosphere 
the camp lives and moves and has its 
being. He does it through the selection 
of staff and his instructions to them. 
He does it through the example he and 
his family present. He “creates” the 
values according to which all things 
are measured at his camp. He ani¬ 
mates the personal relationships which 
bind the community together. A camp 
is a little cosmos which springs into life 
suddenly in June and ends as abruptly 
at the end of August. If this universe 
is a living reality, its vibrations will be 
felt throughout the intervening months 
and even through generations to come. 

Some of the creative activity is con¬ 
scious and visible, much is unconscious 
and invisible. The unconscious part is 
sensed best by the outsider who “feels” 
a distinctive spirit permeating the 
whole enterprise. This is what the 
campers take with them but can not 
put into words. 

The conscious and visible activities 
must also be there and are equally 
important and satisfying. No camp 
director can fail to take pride at the 
presentation of awards as the tangible 
expressions of challenges well met. He 
recollects the aimless thrashings of the 


non-swimmer and shares the joy with 
the camper who now smoothly glides 
through the water. He knows that 
through his creative activity, seeds 
have been planted which will grow into 
satisfying activities in later life. 
Through the mastery of skills, confi¬ 
dence has been instilled in a timid ego 
which will provide courage in all other 
tasks of life. Through his creative 
leadership he hopes to have struck 
some spark in the minds and characters 
of his campers which may burst into 
a living witness of the values held up 
at camp. 

If I were to stop directing our camp 
now I would look back with satisfac¬ 
tion that for two summers at least we 
operated a “Fall Camp”. This in¬ 
volved taking some 25 boys after the 
departure of our regular campers. They 
were wards of the Children’s Aid 
Society and members of an orphanage. 
I would recall the two underprivileged 
teenaged boys who were ready to leave 
school prematurely, but returned from 
camp with a new outlook and have 
now embarked on fruitful careers. I 
would reflect with satisfaction that 
somewhere in Canada there stands a 
monument of stone, long to outlast us 
all, commemorating not only the un¬ 
known soldier but the unsung civilian 
heroes, Ponacka’s monument to the 
“Unknown Gentleman”. 

When at the intimation of death, we 
shall pass our life under review, the 
irritation with the slovenly dishwasher 
or the leaky tank will be forgotten. 
But there will remain the satisfaction 
that parts of oneself have become part 
of the stream of life and that creation 
is not an ended and sealed but a con¬ 
stantly renewed process. That is why 
I am happy to direct a camp. 


Two little booklets worth noting have recently come to hand: 

When You Are In The Woods — by Fay Welch — issued by the State 
University College of Forestry, Syracuse. 

Rigid Frames for Fir Plywood Structures—issued by the Plywood Manufac¬ 
turers’ Association of B.C., 550 Burrard St., Vancouver, B.C. 


Toronto, Canada, June 1962 


141 



Part Two . . . 


CAMP WOODLANDS 

and How To Look After Them 

c: H. IRWIN, 
Camp Shenvood Forest . 


In an introductory article in the 
April issue, forest protection was listed 
as the most important measure. 

The three requisites of fire are fuel, 
heat and air, and by depriving it of 
any or all of these it may be controlled 
and extinguished. It is just the op¬ 
posite process to human resuscitation 
which strives to introduce air to the 
lungs and warmth to the body, but in 
both cases, time is all important. 

In the woods, combustible material 
is ever accumulating with the drying 
and decaying of vegetation which en¬ 
riches and mulches the soil. The well 
kept network of trails and roads pre¬ 
viously mentioned, provides areas free 
of such material where fire may be 
starved and combatted more easily and 
via which men and equipment may be 
shifted quickly. Of course, all areas 
used for camp or cooking fires should 
be cleared to the mineral soil for a 
radius of five feet or more and com¬ 
bustible material should not be left 
where the prevailing wind would carry 
embers. 

If a fire occurs before or after the 
regular camping season, such as today, 
Easter Saturday, one must rely for de¬ 
tection and suppression on mainten¬ 
ance staff (if it has not requested the 
week end off), local residents, munici¬ 
pal officials or forest rangers, depend¬ 
ing on the local set up. It is well to 
have discussed the situaton with them 
so that one may know what to expect 
should a fire occur. If one spots a fire 
and has any doubt of his ability to ex¬ 
tinguish it, he should reach the nearest 
telephone as fast as he can. Much 


better to have more men and equip¬ 
ment arrive on the scene than neces¬ 
sary, than to have the fire get away. 
Just consider the cost of bringing the 
extra men and equipment as a form 
of insurance premium. However, as 
soon as help has been called, get busy. 
Don’t stand back awaiting help that 
may be delayed. A case comes to mind 
of a couple of dozen people idly watch¬ 
ing a fire spread over more than an 
acre of rather open brush while await¬ 
ing a fire pump. When it arrived it 
had not enough hose to reach from the 
water supply, but in the meatime two 
men brought the fire under control by 
beating with wet car rugs. 

With this very dry spring in mind 
and news of many grass fires, we have 
just taken the time to see that our own 
equipment is ready for action—shovels, 
axes, rakes, pails, pack pump and light 
weight gasoline forestry pump, hose, 
suction hose and strainer. Started up 
the engne to make sure it would func¬ 
tion and set aside gas and oil. It may 
have been well that we did so too, be¬ 
cause looking out of my front window 
while writing this, I spotted a fisher¬ 
man almost to his waist in the water 
of the river mouth and behind him on 
the shore a dandy flaming fire. True, 
it was on the sand a few feet from the 
woods, but the first high wind of the 
season was breaking up the ice on the 
lake and fairly lifting the flames to¬ 
ward the dry leaf slope of the neigh¬ 
boring property. We have put out two 
fires on that slope in previous years. 


142 


Canadian Camping 



There are some specialized tools and 
pieces of equipment in addition to 
those mentioned but they are found 
at forest ranger headquarters or a 
large municipal shed. An adjustable 
fog nozzle for a fire pump is much more 
effective in wetting down a wide area 
than the standard nozzle, provided one 
can approach close to the fire. 

When possible, a frontal attack is 
most effective. Flames may be subdued 
with water and if there is no heavy 
fuel, the fire put out. Back pack pumps 
are much more effective and economi¬ 
cal of water than buckets—often they 
can put a small fire out before a power 
pump is set up to deliver water. Earth 
or sand, if available, can be used to 
smother stubborn spots and the trench 
dug up to obtain it makes a fire line. 
Smouldering stumps, logs and roots 
should be kept suppressed until they 
can be properly dealt with. In rocky 
regions smouldering fragments may 
be dislodged and thrown back, but 
water is the main weapon. Spring 
toothed rakes are handy to clear a fire 
break in leaves or light trash. In heavy 
duff or dry muskeg, fire may smoulder 
for ages and must be watched for a 
long time until every spot is dead out. 

If not possible to meet the fire head 
on, a flanking attack can be very 
effective in veering the fire to where 
less damage may be done or by attack¬ 
ing on both flanks, it may be pinched 
off. 

Take advantage of topography and 
if possible, try to avoid fighting fire on 
up grades where it creates its own 
draft and moves faster, often sending 
burning brands to start fires behind the 
fire fighters. 

During the camp season, the picture 
is different. Unless the property is 
very large there should be less chance 
of a bush fire getting away without 
being discovered. At such time all 
camp water pipes and storage tanks 
are filled. At frequent intervals along 
these pipes should be hose taps and at 


least 100 foot lengths of hose available 
for attachment thereto. Equipment 
must be kept safe from tampering and 
yet within easy reach of quite a num¬ 
ber of staff members who know how to 
use it. 

In times of low humidity and high 
fire hazard, smoking by anyone while 
travelling in the woods should be pro¬ 
hibited. It may be well to organize 
night patrols of counsellors and staff- 
two man teams on two hour shifts' 
have been found to work well here 
with a definite route to cover, stressing 
such areas as highways, roads and 
trails, shore and borders of adjoining 
properties. Over a period of years, 
four incipient fires have been found by 
these patrols, all caused by careless 
smokers along highway or road but 
one started by a camp picnic group in 
a rocky place where an old root had 
not been extinguished by the water 
poured over it and it had smouldered 
up a grade between the rocks. 

There should be a plan of action 
known to all. A signal should bring 
all campers to a pre-arranged safe area 
where staff personnel have been detail¬ 
ed to supervise them. The remainder 
of the staff should have definite duties 
to carry out under the one appointed 
to take charge. 

There are usually enough staff mem¬ 
bers to act as fire fighting crew. If in 
any doubt, call for outside aid. In the 
excitement and turmoil that generally 
goes with an emergency, the fire fight¬ 
ers might be greatly hampered if camp¬ 
ers were allowed to get in on the act, 
strongly tempted as they would be to 
do so, and with the best intentions. 
There might be a situation where older 
campers could lend a helpnig hand on 
such jobs as bucket brigade or in prov¬ 
ing the truth of the adage about throw¬ 
ing a “wet blanket” on a project. A 
group with wet blankets working along 
the flank of a fire can do wonders. 
Under certain conditions with light 
tinder and strong wind, more may be 
turn to page 160 


Toronto, Canada, June 1962 


143 



THE CHANCING HEALTH PICTURE 

]. H. EBBS, M.D., 

Taylor St at ten Camps 


A Summer Camp is a healthy ex¬ 
perience, generally speaking, but there 
are calculated risks, no matter where 
a group of energetic children is 
assembled. Small scrapes, splinters, in¬ 
sect bites, sprains, and an occasional 
more serious injury can be expected. 
In a study done a few years ago, we 
found that 71% of such minor injuries 
occurred in the month of July, and 
only 29% in the month of August, 
suggesting that the campers were per¬ 
haps better acclimatised as the summer 
wore on. Another finding, which was 
not unexpected, was that twice as 
many minor accidents and injuries 
occurred in younger girls, as compared 
with older girls, and a staff member 
suffered only half as many. 

The tabulation of infections of all 
kinds from simple skin infections to 
colds and fevers, again showed that 
twice as many occurred in July as in 
August, although this is by no means 
always true. The incidence of infec¬ 
tions in younger campers was twice 
as great as in older campers and staff 
members. This would indicate that the 
younger child perhaps has less immun¬ 
ity, less stamina, or perhaps is more 
susceptible to fatigue. 

The prevention of accidents of all 
types is a major concern in every camp. 
The inspection of the camp by the 
Director and Doctor, staff training, and 
conditioning programmes will help to 
eliminate hazards and increase stamina. 

The common sense practices during 
tripping are the responsibility of the 
staff. The hazards of unknown water 


for swimming are well known to 
trained camp leaders. The crossing of 
water in storms is partly common sense 
and partly experience. Lightning is a 
definite hazard both on the water and 
in exposed areas on land. 

Foresight is often necessary in order 
that emergencies can be satisfactorily 
dealt with. An inspection of the camp 
site, particularly the waterfront and 
swimming areas should include the 
working out of a plan of procedure to 
be followed in the event that resuscita¬ 
tion procedures will have to be fol¬ 
lowed. A recent report in the Journal 
of the American Medical Association 
recounts the experience of a doctor 
who was called to a beach to adminis¬ 
ter to a child who had been submerged 
in the water. Upon arrival, he found a 
trained first-aider giving satisfactory 
mouth-to-nose resuscitation. On exam¬ 
ination the child’s heart could not be 
detected. The doctor immediately 
started external cardiac massage, while 
the first-aider continued with mouth- 
to-nose resusciation. An ambulance 
was called. However, the ambulance 
could not get closer than fifty yards to 
the beach.. It was necessary to impro¬ 
vise a stretcher, and after careful in¬ 
struction the mouth-to-nose resuscita¬ 
tion and external cardiac massage were 
continued without interruption, while 
the victim was transported on the 
stretcher to the ambulance. During 
the trip to the hospital the same pro¬ 
cedure continued uninterrupted, and 
in the meantime the hospital was ready 
to receive the victim. An operation was 
performed, internal cardiac massage 


144 


Canadian Camping 



was carried on by the doctor and a 
tube put through the larynx and 
resuscitation administered directly to 
the child. 

Surveys of drowning accidents in¬ 
dicate that very few occur in properly 
supervised places of recreation such as 
camps. However, the increasing haz¬ 
ards due to water skiing, scuba diving, 
etc., demand that camp directors con¬ 
tinually evaluate and establish safety 
practices when such water-activities 
are introduced. Before water skiing is 
made part of a camping programme, 
the hazards, cost, and need for strict 
supervision of operating practices 
should be considered. The same is true 
of under-water diving. 

In recent years, the press has brought 
to the attention of camping people the 
fact that every summer a large number 
of persons receive bites or stings from 
wasps and other insects. Occasionally, 
in very sensitive individuals, they will 
cause a violent reaction and sometimes 
death. The camp doctor should give 
instructions regarding the handling of 
these cases which are emergencies. 
Persons who are known to be suscep¬ 
tible should be advised by the camp 
doctor and possibly carry medication 
with them. The same is true of those 
campers who are subject to severe 
attacks of asthma. 

The health authorities have become 
increasingly concerned about the rise 
in the incidence of cancer of the lung, 
thought to be associated with the 
smoking of cigarettes. Physicians in¬ 
terested in children throughout North 
America have agreed to do everything 
possible to influence young people to 
avoid taking up the habit of cigarette 
smoking. Camps can play an impor¬ 
tant part in this campaign, since it is 
estimated that 25 to 40% of young 
people start to smoke during the 
camper age. Most camps have solved 
the problem by having a strict rule 


that there will be no smoking by under¬ 
aged persons in their camp, even 
though the camper has permission from 
his parents. 

Summer time is known to be the 
period in which a number of summer 
infections occur. Recently, medical re¬ 
search has identified a number of 
viruses and other organisms which con¬ 
tribute to the illnesses which occur 
during the summer months. Epidemics 
in camps and summer resorts of the 
condition commonly called “Pink Eye” 
occur from time to time. The persons 
affected usually have a mild sore throat, 
red infected eyes with some discharge. 
They suffer from headache, fever, 
sometimes nausea and vomiting, and 
complain of aching muscles. About one 
third of them also develop infections in 
their ears. Glands in the neck are 
usually found by the doctor. A virus, 
known as A PC has been found to 
account for this condition, and is har¬ 
boured in water. It comes from the 
nose and throat of affected persons, 
and is commonly called “swimming 
pool conjunctivitis.” Studies conducted 
a few years ago in a large boys’ camp 
traced the infection, and it is well 
known that water which is infected will 
produce the disease in a high per¬ 
centage of those who swim in that 
particular area. 

Summer infections are best controlled 
by making sure that drinking water has 
an adequate concentration of chlorine. 
Booster doses of Polio Vaccine should 
be emphasized before the campers 
reach camp. In the event that cases 
of “Pink-Eye” or other summer ‘Flu’ 
infections occur, such as diarrhoea, 
swimming should be decentralized in 
order that surface water will not be the 
source of continuing spread of infection. 

From time to time we are faced with 
patients who have had a direct trans¬ 
fer of infection from animals, through 
turn to page 160

CANOE STROKES 


CANOEING STROKES — A Definition 

At the recent Ontario Camping Conference a demonstration of the canoeing strokes 
included in the various canoe tests levels was given. This article is being offered to provide 
Instructors and Examiners a description of those strokes. This was not an easy task and 
the technical group under the leadership of Doug Lloyd is to be commended for the great 
amount of work that has gone into the preparation of this set of notes. At a later date, 
diagrams to accompany this definitive article will be made available. It may also be 
necessary to alter some of the material following some experience with its use. Your 
comments are invited. 

KIRK A. W. WIPPER, Chairman. 


NOTES 

1. Definitions— 

a. Standing—canoe motionless at the 
beginning of the stroke. 

b. Running — canoe under way 
caused by paddling. 

c. Bow (as prefixed to name of a 
stroke of a bow-man)—executed 
on the same side as his regular 
stroke (i.e. on the left if he is 
paddling on left). 

d. Cross-bow (compare “bow*’ above) 
—executed on the side opposite to 
his regular stroke (i.e. on the 

.right if he is paddling left). 

2. Style—not considered as an element 
in itself except insofar as it might 
affect the competence of the per¬ 
formance, or the efficiency of the 
stroke. The committee was in agree¬ 
ment that some room should be left 
for the expression of individuality in 
style—a feature of the art of canoe¬ 
ing which distinguishes it from other 
recreational sports. 

3. It is to be noted that with one or 
two possible exceptions, none of the 
strokes described involves an inter¬ 
change of hands on the paddle. If 
the right hand is on the grip and the 
left on the shaft before the start of 
the stroke, the two hands are in the 
same relative position during the 
stroke. 


4. It is assumed that all paddlers are 
in a kneeling position (both knees 
down) unless otherwise noted. 

A. BASIC STROKES: 

1. a plain stroke, with the purpose of 
moving the canoe forward. The 
paddle blade is at right angles to the 
canoe during the stroke. Pull back 
with the hand on shaft and press 
forward and downward with hand 
on grip. The recovery is accom¬ 
plished by continuing to press for¬ 
ward and downward then backward 
with the grip hand while the hand 
on the shaft in a simultaneous action 
lifts the blade slightly and then 
swings forward the blade with sur¬ 
face parallel to water, until the start 
position is reached. The stroke is 
resumed by raising the grip hand 
while the hand on the shaft remains 
motionless. 

Notes: 

1. Both hands will be observed to 
travel in a circular motion. 

2. Arms are slightly bent to avoid 
stiffness. 

3. The paddle should not be allowed 
to revolve in the hands. 

4. Care should be taken to make 
sure the same side of the blade is 
always being used as the pressure 
surface. This can be easily accom¬ 
plished in the initial stages of 


146 


Canadian Camping 



learning by a slight bending in of 
both wrists at the moment of re¬ 
entry of the blade after the 
recovery. 

2. “J” Stroke: 

A basic stroke for moving the canoe 
forward and maintaining its motion 
in a straight line. It is to be used 
when paddling alone, or as a stern 
.. stroke with another paddler in the 
. bow. 1 (It ^ust. not be used when 
paddling in the bow.) 

The performance in most respects is 
the same as the “Bow” stroke, dif¬ 
fering only at the completion of the 
“pull” motion. At the moment the 
recovery is started, both wrists are 
revolved forward, causing the blade 
of the paddle to turn to a position 
more or' less parallel to the canoe, 
thus providing a momentary rudder 
action to steer the canoe. The recov¬ 
ery is then effected as before. As a 
canoeist becomes more expert, this 
ruddering action frequently blends 
with the recovery movement, with 
the blade gradually sliding forward 
out of the water as the paddle is 
being prepared for the next stroke. 
The steering in this case is accom¬ 
plished by a slight upward pressure. 

3. fcow Steering Strokes: 

1. Bow Cut—paddle at 30° angle to 
the gunwale; hand on shaft may 
lock thumb oyer gunwale; it is 
important that both wrists bend 
in backwards sharply before start¬ 
ing stroke, causing the former 
“pulling” surface to be now the 
deflecting surface. 

2. Cross-bow cut — paddle at 30° 
angle to gunwale, hand on shaft 
may lock thumb over gunwale; it 
may also slide up shaft somewhat 
for convenience. When paddling 
on left, right hand remains on grip 
while the left locks on gunwale. 
A one hand performance can be 


accomplished by allowing the grip 
hand to slide half way up the shaft 
and grip sliding under the arm. It 
is not necessary then to hold the 
paddle with second hand. A 
thumb lock may be used as before 
if convenient. 

3. Bow Rudder—paddle blade pro¬ 
trudes up to one foot in front of 
canoe, tight against the bow strip 
and with the remainder of the 
blade as close as possible to Can¬ 
vas of canoe, producing an angle 
of about 30° with a line projected 
from the bow. To put the blade 
into position, hold the grip end 

j firmly and reverse the position of 
. the hand on the shaft (with back 
of hand face down), then release 
the hand on the grip and twist the 
. hand on the shaft (back of hand 
facing up) allowing the grip and 
upper portion of shaft to pass 
under the arm; then thrust the 
paddle forward into position de¬ 
scribed above. (Note: it is impor¬ 
tant that this stroke be executed 
between the strokes of the sterns- 
man for effective results.) 

4. Cross-bow rudder — position of 
paddle as in the preceding stroke 
but put into effect by lifting the 
paddle by the hand oh the shaft 
and after leaning forward slightly 
allowing the blade to drop in front 

‘ bf the canoe in the angle described 
' v above. If this is done properly it 
is not necessary to keep the hand 
on the shaft; a light hold on the 
grip is sufficient. (Note: In both 
of these strokes the shaft of the 
paddle should form an angle of 
30-45° with the water, if the 
angle is too large, the blade will 
slip under the canoe). 

B. DRAW STROKES 
NOTES 

These strokes differ from the four 
previous bow strokes in that they 


Toronto, Canada, June 1962 


147 



provide extra momentum. There¬ 
fore they should be considered as 
possible emergency strokes and not 
necessarily tied to the rhythm of 
paddling. They also require con¬ 
siderably more strength and skill; 
for these reasons they should be re¬ 
served for more advanced work. 

The similarity with the “cut" stroke 
should be noted. 

5. Bow Draw 

Type A —paddle in a raised position 
to start, at a 60° angle to water 
blade parallel to canoe. The wrist 
of the hand on shaft should be 
bent backward as far as possible 
(as in bow-cut)—the further the 
better. Insert paddle in water, 
draw in sharply with the hand on 
shaft keeping the hand on the grip 
comparatively steady to provide 
leverage. Recover the paddle by 
deflecting the paddle forward and 
out of the water, then raise paddle 
to starting position. The total 
stroke produces a circular motion. 

Type B —starting as above but tfie 
recovery uses the plain bow stroke. 
Not as violent as “type A”—useful 
for holding canoe into wind, or 
making a gradual turn. 

6. Cross bow draw 

Paddle at start of stroke should form 
a 30-45° angle with gunwale and 
45° angle with the water. The hand 
on the grip should be kept low to 
avoid awkwardness in balance. From 
the ordinary paddling stroke, swing 
the paddle into the described posi¬ 
tion by lowering the grip hand and 
guiding the paddle with the hand 
on shaft in a wide sweeping motion. 
As this stroke requires a sizeable 
reach beyond the gunwale the sweep¬ 
ing motion should be accompanied 
with a counter-balancing shift of the 
weight (hips) to the opposite side 
The paddle is then plied in a circular 


motion (as in Type A draw), draw¬ 
ing in, then recovering by an up¬ 
ward, outward motion. As in the 
draw the bulk of the power comes 
from the action of the hand on the 
shaft. 

C. SPECIAL STROKES 

Standing pry’ (compare pushaway) 

Paddle is inserted at 45° to water 
(if singling this should be done by 
reaching as far beyond the centre 
thwart as practical). The bend in 
the canoe helps to hold paddle in 
position. Blade is flat against canoe. 
Holding the paddle with a hand on 
the grip only and using the gunwale 
as a fulcrum press down and causing 
canoe to move away from paddle in 
a pivoting motion. The stroke if 
short can be easily recovered; twist 
the wrist, turn the blade 90° to 
canoe, then slide paddle back to the 
gunwale, and by a further twist of 
wrist resume original position. It is 
not necessary to remove paddle from 
water. A number of short strokes 
are more effective than one large 
one. 

Running pry: 

Usually a small sweep precedes this 
stroke. 

In the recovery of the paddle which 
is parallel to water push down with 
the hand on grip; the hand on the 
shaft slides up shaft. By the time 
paddle is in forward position, the 
momentum caused by swinging the 
paddle forward has brought the 
hand formerly on the shaft up to 
position. Since the paddle blade is 
flat to water during recovery, with 
the hand which is now at the grip, 
on the side of the grip curl the wrist 
forward so that the blade of paddle 
forms a 45° angle to canoe. The 
hand is in a raised position forming 

turn to page 157

A TYPICAL DAY . . . 


For me, the ideal summer would be 
that of a Cabin Counsellor—the friends 
you will make, the memories you will 
share, the rich dividends in human 
relations that you will gain, will be 
drawn upon all your life. It is not a 
coincidence that so many of our out¬ 
standing men and women of today were 
camp counsellors yesterday. I must 
warn you that there is a magic about 
camping. It gets into your blood and 
once there, you cannot get it out. It 
will stay with you for life. 

Everything said here will not apply 
directly to your particular camp and 
some of it will seem like old stuff to 
you. I will try to point out some of the 
important little extra things that make 
the difference between an excellent 
counsellor and one who just does an 
adequate job. No matter what kind 
of camp you work at, we all have one 
thing in common. We all work with 
children. These children all have the 
same basic needs. Therefore, basic 
things discussed will apply which can 
readily be adapted to your own par¬ 
ticular camp and your own group. 

The greatest single factor that will 
determine the happiness and success 
of a camper’s summer is you, the 
counsellor. You are responsible for 
everything that happens to your camp¬ 
ers twenty-four hours a day. The great¬ 
est asset in working successfully with 
children is the ability to remember 
what it felt like to be a certain age. 
In any situation, ask yourself, “How 
would I have felt at this age?”. 
Secondly, your campers’ behaviour will 


From an address given at the 1962 
Ontario Camping Association 
Conference by BARRY LOWES, 
Director, Camp Timberlane. 


be governed by your example more 
than by anything else, not what you 
tell them, but what you show them. 
You will be judged by your actions, not 
by your words. 

Get Up 

Set a good example from the first 
day. Be the first one up. Bounce out 
of bed. Be cheery. Don’t lie in bed 
and keep yelling at the campers, “Up 
and at ’em, gang”. Once your eyes 
are open, check the weather and dress 
accordingly. Too often I see counsellors 
coming to breakfast in jackets, gloves 
and scarves, while their campers come 
in T-shirts. Long pants and jackets to 
breakfast are safe bets on any day. If 
your campers have to cross a grassy 
field, it is wise to wear rubber boots, 
for a heavy dew can soak shoes better 
than a rain. 

Check your campers for symptoms of 
illness. If your suspicions are aroused, 
be sure to take them to the nurse for 
the morning clinic. Make washing, 
brushing of teeth an hair combing a 
set routine. These are not questioned 
or discussed, you just assume naturally 
that everyone will do them. Morning 
dips under supervision can be fun for 
some. You had better check this policy 
with your camp director. Washing in 
the river or lake can be beautiful 
tradition for a cabin group. Go slowly 
and quietly, pausing for a moment at 
the water’s edge to listen and watch. 
It is a beautiful way to begin any day. 


Toronto, Canada, June 1962 


149 



When you start for breakfast, don't 
leave any stragglers behind. All go 
together. If the campers tend to pair 
off. then you should walk with the 
“loner”, the camper who is left out. 
One counsellor should stay behind and 
routinely pull back the covers on each 
bed. From time to time you will find 
a wet bed that is being hidden by a 
camper. If you don’t follow this 
routine, then only your nose will finally 
tell you after several days. If you find 
a wet bed, strip it immediately and 
take the wet linens to the laundry. 
Re-make it so that no one knows. There 
is no need for it to be public knowledge. 
Treat bed wetting matter-of-factly, as 
an accident that could happen to any¬ 
one. Beware of teasing and ridicule by 
the other campers. Here again, your 
attitude will set the tone. If the acci¬ 
dent is repeated, start a program with 
the camper to limit his intake of 
liquids after supper, to lift him during 
the night and again early in the morn¬ 
ing if necessary. 

Meals 

With hepatitis on the increase, it is 
vitally important that all campers wash 
their hands after toileting and before 
all meals. Check them, don’t assume 
that they have all washed. 

While the method of food sendee 
varies from camp to camp, certain 
general responsibilities will be the same. 
Always serve the campers first. A 
counsellor never heaps up his plate and 
then passes the remainder along to the 
campers. It is probably best if you 
serve the campers. This guarantees a 
fair share plus variety for everyone. 
Left to their own choice, most campers 
will eat meat and potatoes but few 
vegetables. 

The manners of your campers will be 
determined by the tone that you set 
during the first few days of camp. Set 
your expectations high. As in all be¬ 
haviour, you will generally get what 
they think you expect of them. They 


will test you in manners as in all 
discipline. Don’t nag, be firm but 
pleasant. At the outset, squelch grab¬ 
bing, yelling, using hands, mixing all 
their food into one pile of mush or 
deliberately spilling things to gain 
attention. Some campers will bolt their 
food as though they feared losing it to 
some one else. They may have sound 
reasons and experiences at home to 
justify their behaviour. Make it clear 
that there will be anough for everyone 
and that no seconds will be served 
until everyone has finished their firsts 
anyway. 

Discourage the campers who says 
“Ugh!”, when some food comes on the 
table or who makes a face or some 
other distasteful comment. As a coun¬ 
sellor, you should never criticize the 
food by word, expression, or gesture. 
If you feel that some thing is wrong, 
tell the director later. He is the only 
one who can set this situation right. 

Never chastise a camper in front 
of the others nor cause him to lose face. 
Sit the worst offender beside you where 
you can control him without disturbing 
the other campers. Never, never, never 
dock food. By “dock” I mean withhold 
food. Desserts are the favourite “boot- 
screw” of poor counsellors. Food is not 
a privilege, food is a right. If a camper 
is misbehaving to that extent, perhaps 
you should have him sit quietly and eat 
after the others have left. If you ever 
feel that it is necessary to withhold 
food, discuss it with the director first. 
Never threaten or force anyone to eat. 
Campers should be encouraged to trv 
a little of everything but never forced. 
Often a well meaning counsellor will 
ioad up a small child’s plate. This can 
overwhelm a child. It is better to serve 
smaller portions and have the camper 
ask for seconds. I can find no justifica¬ 
tion for witholding a camper’s dessert 
because he does not finish all of the 
main course. A meal consists of several 
courses and he is entitled to all of them. 


150 


Canadian Camping 



On the other hand, he should not be 
allowed to fill up on extra desserts. If 
you, as a counsellor, feel that a camper 
is not eating enough or the right things, 
consult the nurse. Children never 
deliberately starve themselves to death, 
although parents and young counsellors 
have been known to worry themselves 
almost to death. Beware of young 
girls on diets. They all want to look 
like Debbie Reynolds. Even the ninety 
pound ones want to diet. Dieting should 
only be permitted under the direction 
of her family doctor, her parents and 
the camp medical staff. 

Do not permit campers to take any 
food from the dining hall, either for a 
sick camper or a tired counsellor. If 
there are any extra desserts, they must 
be shared equally and fairly, not kept 
for the counsellors alone. See that your 
campers salt their food for they lose a 
great deal of salt through perspiration 
in the summer which must be replaced. 

If you have a new or shy camper, 
sit him beside you. The first few meals 
can be overwhelming for a new camper. 
If you sit him at the far end of the 
table, he may starve. Mealtime should 
be a time for fun and conversation that 
is interesting, light and on a high plane. 
However, when someone asks for quiet, 
keep your group quiet. So often I see 
counsellors at a table with their hands 
raised for quiet, but their tongues going 
a mile a minute. 

Clean Up 

Clean up can be drudgery or a 
simple necessity, depending upon you. 
Again, your attitude is all important. 
I suggest that you adopt the attitude 
of “Let’s do it fast and well and get it 
over with”. Try to establish pride in 
your cabin. If you play the role of 
Simon Degree, they will outlast you, I 
promise. Make a duty chart or wheel 
that has each person’s name on it and 
the duties for each day of the week. 
Be sure that you add your name to it. 
It is a good idea to have one camper as 


supervisor each day. This spreads the 
role of “dirty guy” around. Besides 
campers get a big kick out of being able 
to inspect your bed and shelves. 

Clean up can afford young campers 
an ideal oportunity to help one another. 
You should move about helping them, 
joking, talking, making it fun. Sweep¬ 
ing is difficult for young campers. You 
may have to go back over it later. 
Beware of the young campers who strip 
their beds, throw the sheets, pillow and 
blankets oil the floor and then walk all 
over them while they make their beds. 
It happens. 

You must inspect campers’ shelves 
regularly. Without thinking, young 
campers will stuff wet shorts, bathing 
suits or other damp clothing into the 
back of their shelves, trunks or laundry 
bags. If this happens, you will have 
a wonderful crop of mildew within 
a few days that can ruin clothing. You 
must also be on guard against the 
camper who has an accident in his 
pants and hides them in his laundry 
bag. 

One day per week, Laundry day is 
often the best day, have a super clean 
up, that is, strip your beds, shake out 
and air your blankets. Take everything 
out ol your shelves or your trunks and 
repack them. You will me amazed at 
what you will find. 

Programme 

Programme is everything that hap¬ 
pens during any twenty-four hours not 
just at activity periods. If you are 
sensitive and imaginative, you will see 
activity possibilities that others miss. 
Camping is exciting; by its very nature 
it is filled with adventure; hiking, 
exploring, rafting, swimming, and 
sleeping out, but adventurous does 
not mean dangerous. Safety must be 
uppermost in your mind at all times. 
There are two extremes that should be 
avoided. One is the cot ton-wool world 
that is over-protective. The other is 
the flagrantly dangerous that courts 


Toronto , Canada, June 1962 


151 



injury. We have a saying at camp 
“If in doubt, don’t do it”. You must 
learn to anticipate hazards and thereby 
avoid them, such as glass, nails, metal, 
broken equipment, etc. These should 
be removed, repaired or reported. 
Things like knives arc for campcraft, 
not for throwing. If they use them 
unwisely, they may have to lose the 
privilege of using them. Painful acci¬ 
dents can be avoided by always using 
a flashlight at night. Safety should be 
taught as an integral part of any 
activity. Teach basic first-aid to your 
campers. They are interested and learn 
readily. 

Most youngsters seem to like to 
rough-house, but this should never be 
done inside the cabin, because it 
invariably ends in someone getting hurt 
and the rest saying “We’re sorry”. 
I hate the word “sorry”. Instead of 
inside the cabin, take the group out on 
the beach and have a good rumble and 
let off that extra steam. In safety, as 
in all else, your example is most 
important. 

During the first few days at camp, 
try to devise activities that will draw 
your cabin group together, such as a 
cabin project, a hike, a cook-out, some 
adventure that is shared. Make up a 
cabin name, song and yell. Your camp 
will have its own particular method of 
programming. I would like to mention 
briefly a few important extras. 

Too often when choosing activities, 
democracy is considered to be majority 
rule. This is a common fallacy. True 
democracy is not a matter of the 
majority out voting the minority all 
summer. 

When going to an activity, be on 
time. If you are late, it shortens the 
period and spoils the lesson. Help the 
instructor if you can with the instruc¬ 
tion or at least help him to control the 
group. Remember that you should 
know your campers best. Join in the 
activities with your campers. Let your 


hair down. Activities take on new zest 
for campers when you participate with 
them. Besides, you enjoy yourself also. 
Play with your campers at times other 
than your schedule periods, particularly 
at those free times before meals. 

At the end of any activity period, 
you should ask yourself these questions. 
Was it fun? What did they learn? 
How could the activity have been 
improved? Where will it lead us or is 
it a dead-end activity? What happened 
of significance to the campers? 

General Swim 

Every camper will not want to go to 
every general swim. However, if it 
becomes habitual, look for a deeper 
reason why. If for some good reason a 
camper does not want to go to general 
swim, encourage him to pursue some 
other interest, certainly not lying on his 
bed with a comic book. 

Know where your campers are at all 
limes. Campers should be permitted to 
wander by themselves or in pairs within 
a defined area at times, but you should 
know generally where they are going 
to be. If you do not have lifeguard 
duty, take advantage of the opportunity 
to swim with your group. They will 
love it. Play games in the shallow area. 
Buddy-up with the “loner” or play 
with the non-swimmer in the first area. 
When the swim is over, be sure that 
they dry well, especially their heads, 
put on shoes and hurry back to the 
cabin to get out of clammy bathing 
suits. The period after general swim is 
a vulnerable time. When the group 
gets back to the cabin, if it is unsuper¬ 
vised, the underdog will be picked on, 
there will be towel flicking, water fights, 
teasing, raiding, fights, and rough¬ 
housing. These undesirable activities 
are most common at this time. There¬ 
fore, it is vitally important to be with 
your group. 

Health 

A camper who spends too long in the 
health center is going to have his 


152 


Canadian Campinq 



summer spoiled. Consequently, it is 
important that you do not ignore nor 
minimize small cuts or symptoms of 
illness. A little antiseptic and a band- 
aid today are far better than penicil¬ 
lin and hot compresses tomorrow. 
Campers are too busy to bother. You 
must remind and in fact, see that these 
things are looked after promptly. Do 
not send a camper to the nurse, take 
him yourself. If you don’t, he will 
probably wander out of sight, lean 
against the tree, then come back later 
and say “The nurse says Tm fine”. 

Never diagnose and never treat, not 
even an Aspirin. Tin afraid than Ben 
Casey is going to spawn a number 
of embryo doctors this summer. If 
campers bring medicines to camp, they 
should be turned in promptly to the 
nurse. The medical staff is there be¬ 
cause of their highly specialized skill 
and knowledge. Use them. If the 
nurse tells you to bring a camper back 
at a certain time or to see that some¬ 
thing is done, follow her instructions 
carefully. 

If the camper is confined to the 
medical center, find our the visiting 
hours and don't miss any opportunities 
to visit. That camper needs you. Try 
to bring a book, game, flower, anything 
of interest that will brighten his day. 
Most important of all is your cheerful 
presence. Perhaps his cabin mates 
could make a get-well card or write a 
group letter. They may even be per¬ 
mitted to talk through a screen window 
from a distance, if this will not disturb 
other patients. Once the camper is 
permitted to return to the group, you 
must see that there is a balance between 
rest and exercise for a few days. Follow 
the nurse’s instructions. Campers will 
usually be too ambitious and want to 
overdo it. 

Cleanliness 

The most honorable camper will slip 
up when it comes to cleanliness. They 
are just too busy. Don’t assume that 


because you tell them to go and wash 
that it will be done. This is wishful 
thinking. Make going to the toilet, 
washing and brushing their teeth a 
routine. When the whole cabin group 
gathers at the lake or around the wash 
stand, it can become a lot of fun. 
Unobtrusively check them and make 
light of sending someone back to dig 
out that extra dirt. Joke along with 
them. A clean counsellor with good 
health habits begets clean campers. 
The familiar cry heard from campers 
is “we swim every day, who needs to 
wash”. A hot soap bath, that is a 
shower or even a sponge bath with 
water heated over an open fire, should 
be taken at least three times a week, 
including the hair. 



Clothing 

You must see that your campers 
change their clothes regularly. This 
means girls too. They can be just as 
lazy when it comes to cleanliness. Un¬ 
derwear and socks should be changed 
daily. If your campers have enough 
clothing, it is a good idea to have them 
put everything into their laundry bags 
when they undress at night and put on 
clean clothes in the morning. There is 
no reason why a director should sec 
Monday’s mustard on Friday’s shirt. 
Discourage the borrowing and lending 
of clothing, particularly bathing suits. 
Counsellors should never borrow from 


Toronto , Canada , June 1962 


153 


campers, whether it is clothing, flash¬ 
lights, or any other camp equipment. 

Check to see that campers do not 
wear damp bathing suits or clothing all 
day. When left on, they can produce 
a rash or chill. As wonderful as the 
sun is, it can be a crippler if campers 
are over-exposed. See that your camp¬ 
ers wear sun hats, especially when they 
are out in boats. Gradually increase 
their exposure to the sun, rather than 
have them sufTer from sunburn. In¬ 
sects are a part of camp life. Tender 
campers should be protected in the 
early evening and on muggy days from 
mosquitoes, by pulling their socks over 
their long pants and by wearing long- 
sleeved shirts that are done up at the 
wrists and neck. 

Over-fatigue can be a big camp 
problem for programmes can be highly 
charged, if the activity is too intensive, 
too competitive, and unbalanced. Al¬ 
low time for relaxation and leisurely 
activities that provide a change of 
pace. 

Rest Hour 

Rest hour means rest. The campers 
need it. This is the time to recharge 
their batteries. Rest hour must be well 
supervised. It works best when there 
is a counsellor in the cabin. Take ad¬ 
vantage of the opportunity to rest 
yourself. Don’t insist on absolute si¬ 
lence, only consideration for the others 
who might want to rest. Some may 
nap, others may write letters, read, 
play quiet games or tell stories. Rest 
hour does not mean swinging from the 
rafters, trampolining on beds, running 
errands, horseplay, etc. Perhaps on a 
hot day the group could sit or lie out¬ 
side in the shade. Lying on his back, a 
straw between his teeth, gazing up 
through the pine trees at the white 
clouds scudding, can be a wonderful 
experience for any camper. Perhaps 
a guitar and some soft singing have 
their place. Rest hour need not be a 


prison; with imagination it can be 
transformed into restful, memorable 
hours. 

Letters 

Your camp will probably have a pol¬ 
icy concerning regular letter writing 
days for campers. “What shall I say?” 
you will be asked repeatedly. Help them 
to tell of their camp accomplishments, 
things they have done, friends made, 
and new experiences. While censor¬ 
ship of campers’ mail is to be deplored* 
their writing can certainly be helped 
and guided. If you were a parent, 
what would you want to know? 

Be sure that the address is clearly 
written, to ensure its delivery at the 
other end. If one of your campers does 
not receive mail for several days, dis¬ 
cuss the matter wih the director. If 
the situation is serious enough, it might 
even warrant you writing him a card 
from town on your day off. 

Rain 

Of one thing you can be certain, at 
some time during the summer, it is 
going to rain. Whether these days will 
be a bane or a boon will depend on 
how well prepared you are. Loneli¬ 
ness can creep in, or teasing, arguing, 
and fighting can result from being too 
closely confined for hours. As with 
everything else in camp, your attitude 
and example are all important. They 
set the tone, so be cheerful, bright and 
dress colourfully. If you ever feel the 
need to coast, do it on a sunny day. 
Rainy days demand and require your 
reserves of patience, cheerfulness, ener¬ 
gy and resourcefulness. Treat rainy 
days as opportunities for a change of 
pace—have ideas and games up your 
sleeve that are used only on rainy days. 

It never rains out of a blue sky. Be 
alert to changes in the weather, e.g. 
darkening skies, changing winds, a ring 
around the moon, etc., and take steps 
that will save you problems once rain 
comes. Make sure that your tent flaps 
or cabin shutters are fastened down. 


154 


Canadian Camping 



Slacken the tent ropes slightly. Clear 
all clothes from your clothesline. They 
can be hung out again after the rain. 
Take in sleeping bags or blankets that 
are airing. Make sure your firewood is 
well covered. Finally, check the 
grounds around your cabin for any¬ 
thing the rain could hurt. 

During the rain your first responsi¬ 
bility is to see that your campers are 
dressed properly in raincoats, hats and 
boots. If it is cold, wear a jacket or 
sweater also. Each year more and 
more wise counsellors are taking um¬ 
brellas to camp. At first the campers 
may scoff at you, but in a rain there 
are always some who sidle up to you 
and say “can I get under, too?”. 

Evening Programmes 

I will not discuss activities for even¬ 
ing programmes—this is another large 
topic in itself. At all evening pro¬ 
grammes, it is important that you be 
with your group and sit with them, not 
with other counsellors at the back. 
Keep your group under control and 
attentive if others are running the pro¬ 
gramme. Participate with them if this 
is called for. Towards the end of the 
evening, taper off the excitement. Try 
to end on a quieter mood. Don’t let 
campers get over-tired or over-stimu¬ 
lated just before bedtime. End the day 
with taps or some other suitable ritual. 
It can be very beautiful, impressionable 
and memorable for your campers. 
Leave the evening programme in ample 
time to allow for snacks and prepara¬ 
tion for bed without rushing and 
nagging. 

Bedtime 

Bedtime is the most important 45 
minutes of the day. Don’t be what I 
call a “pull-chain” counsellor, that is, 
one who hurries his campers into bed, 
pulls the light out and disappears. 
Don’t short-change your campers dur¬ 
ing this most impressionable time of 
the day. 

Our cabin always had a small cabin 
fire ready, covered with a ground sheet 


and a small supply of firewood to one 
side, also covered. We didn’t use it 
every evening but it was always ready 
when the time seemed opportune. 
There is something warm, intimate and 
magnetic about a small fire shared by 
a cabin group. We used to sit around 
it, reviewing the day and planning for 
tomorrow. Sometimes we would have 
a quiet song, or a snack, but often a 
snack can destroy the mood that you 
are trying to create. At the end of this 
10 or 15 minutes we used to stand and 
put our arms around the shoulders of 
the person next to us and all look into 
the fire for a few moments of silence 
and meditation. We ended with a 
prayer that was our own cabin prayer. 
No one spoke or broke the silence until 
we were back inside the cabin. 

Go to the wash house together as a 
group. Count heads, make a routine 
of this. Do not make the common mis¬ 
take of having children brush their 
teeth, get into bed and then give them 
a candy or snack. 

Check your boys, many of them will 
want to wear their underwear under 
their pajamas. This is not a healthy 
practice. Check the warmth of your 
campers. On cold nights, I would 
suggest that they put on a pair of 
clean socks, sweatshirt or sweater. By 
doubling the lower blanket in two and 
putting the top blanket singly over it 
to bind it in, you can create three 
thicknesses from two blankets. Dis¬ 
courage the nightly use of a sleeping 
bag for camp periods longer than 10 
to 14 days. Most sleeping bags do not 
have a removable lining so that it 
becomes dirty and unhealthy from pro¬ 
longed use. If a sleeping bag is used, 
it should be aired often in direct sun¬ 
light. Campers should not be permitted 
to sleep together. It is too crowded 
and it is also a psychologically vulner¬ 
able situation. 

Prayers should be a natural part of 
going to bed. Unfortunately, many 
teenage counsellors are going through 


Toronto , Canada , June 1962 


155 



a self-conscious period about prayers. 
This is unfortunate because, as in 
everything else, your attitude and prac¬ 
tice will set the tone. It is best if you 
kneel and pray with them. If you can¬ 
not bring yourself to do this, at least 
set aside a quiet period with the lights 
out during which time each can pray 
in his own way. If some do not wish 
to pray, then they should just lie 
quietly and respect the rights of others. 

Once the lights are out, take five 
minutes to go quietly from bed to bed. 
Sitting on the edge of their beds, speak 
to each camper briefly, quietly, confi¬ 
dentially and reassuringly. Talk about 
some highlight of particular signifi¬ 
cance to him that occurred during the 
day. Congratulate him on some deed 
or gesture that he might feel went 
unnoticed. If he was upset by some¬ 
thing during the day, clarify it and 
reassure him. Leave a camper feeing 
secure, wanted, and warm inside by 
always ending on a pleasant note. Put 
their worlds together for them. This 
can be a lonely time of day for some. 
Five minutes spent wisely each night 
like this will pay greater dividends 
than anything else that you do as a 
counsellor. Don’t miss the opportunity. 
I have used this successfully with every 
age group from 6 to 16. 

Spiritual Values 

I didn’t discuss spiritual values un¬ 
der any particular part of the day 
because they are learned all day, all 
week, any time, not just at services. 
There are innumerable, impressionable, 
teachable moments that occur each 
day. The sensitive, alert counsellor 
will catch them. 

Spiritual values are caught, not 
taught. Pause on the way back to the 
cabin to gaze at the sky, or stop and 
listen to the night sounds. Sometimes 
the silence can be deafening. A fledg¬ 
ling that has fallen from the nest, a 
delicate flower, the chance to cheat or 


play fair, to lie or tell the truth, to 
steal, to help and so on and on these 
indelible moments that shape attitudes, 
habits and values arise before you and 
your campers. If you let them slip by, 
your campers will be just a little 
poorer because of it. 

God seems to be just a little bit 
closer at camp. Sometimes He seems 
hard to find in our cities with the 
hectic pace, the complexities, the pres¬ 
sures, the gaudiness. Camp is stripped 
of these trappings, our opportunities 
for imparting spiritual values are, 
therefore, greater. 

A counsellor affects eternity, he 
never knows how far his influence will 
spread. The greatest single factor in 
determining the happiness and success 
of any summer is you, the counsellor. 
It is a tremendous responsibility that 
you take on. If it seems too great, do 
not become a camp counsellor. But if 
you have the courage, the vision, the 
ability to learn, then come on in, the 
water’s fine. You won't be left to sink 
or swim. There are many hands ready 
to help you. Beware though, for camp 
is an infectious disease and, once you 
catch it, it will be in your blood for 
life. 

Disraeli once said, “Youth is the 
guardian of posterity”. Just think for 
a moment, the children who come to 
camp to-day will be running this 
country in the year 2000. Man has 
exploded into space. In just over 50 
years we have come from the Wright 
brothers to Colonel Glenn. Who has an 
imagination wild enough to speculate 
on what the year 2000 will hold in 
store for these children? By helping 
children to meet each day’s living on a 
full, rich and adequate basis, we can 
best prepare them to meet their later 
life. 

It is a tremendous responsibility, but 
also a tremendous opportunity for all 
of us.

from page 148 

a 45° angle to water. The momen¬ 
tum of the canoe carries the canoe 
around. 

This is primarily a “singling” stroke, 
although it could be used in the bow 
as an advanced form of the bow 
rudder. 

Backwater: 

Without changing the grip of either 
hand swing the paddle backward 
(reverse of recovery in bow stroke), 
insert paddle and draw forward. The 
same surface of the paddle should be 
used to draw as in the bow stroke if 
properly done. 

Pushaway: 

Insert paddle close to canoe at 90° 
angle to water with blade parallel 
to canoe and using gunwale as ful¬ 
crum pull down on grip, causing the 
canoe to move sideways away from 
paddle. Recover by twisting wrists 
so that blade is 90° to canoe, slide 
paddle in to canoe and resume orig¬ 
inal position. (Compare standing 

pry-) 

Standing Draw: 

Reaching outward with both arms, 
insert paddle and draw in with hand 
on shaft. Recover by lifting the 
paddle up and out. As in all the 
draw strokes, the hand on shaft 
pulls, while the hand on grip pushes. 
Draws canoe to paddle. 

Feathering: 

This is really a continuous draw 
stroke. Insert paddle as in draw 
stroke. Draw in. Instead of remov¬ 
ing blade from water allow the wrist 
of the hand on shaft to bend first 
forward then backward, with an 
alternating sideways motion, taking 
care to maintain the drawing pres¬ 
sure. The similarity of this stroke to 


a figure eight on its side is worth 
noting. More pressure on one side of 
the eight will cause the canoe to 
swing. 

Reverse Feathering: 

As in feathering, except that in place 
of the draw in pressure substitute a 
press out pressure. 

Front sweep: 

With the paddle held almost parallel 
to water, start stroke as far forward 
as possible and continue as far back 
as practical. Allowing the hand on 
shaft to slip slightly up the shaft, 
permits a wider and thus more effec¬ 
tive sweep. The most useful part of 
the sweep is the first 120° of the 
circle; it is not advisable to carry 
paddle much further as it only makes 
recovery difficult. 

Reverse sweep: 

a. As the above but all actions re¬ 
versed. For better support, it is 
recommended to reverse the hold 
on shaft in such a way that the 
hand is below and behind shaft. 

b. with underwater recovery, at the 
end of stroke, twist the wrist on 
shaft, thus turning blade parallel 

* to canoe. Slide the blade tight to 
canoe by raising the hand on grip 
and drawing back the hand on 
shaft. Let wrist of hand on shaft 
assume the first (reversed) posi¬ 
tion at the first forward motion of 
the next stroke. 

Stern draw: 

Action as in bow draw type B. The 
shaft should be straight up and down 
at end of stroke. The blade at least 
parallel to gunwale or forming an 
angle with the forward part of canoe 
(not the reverse. This is most im¬ 
portant as before the stroke is made

Council Ring Ceremonies 
und Fires 

B. M. TAYLOR, 
West Vancouver, B.C, 


Campfires, Ceremonies and Dances 
have special significance in the Indian 
program of a camp. They should be 
infrequent enough to be looked for¬ 
ward to and back upon, as special oc¬ 
casions in the programme. The eti¬ 
quette of the council should be thor¬ 
oughly understood and followed. Rules 
and regulations are simple and consist 
merely of good manners. Do not de¬ 
grade the ceremony with the use of 
pidgin-English as the Indian himself 
did not talk in this manner, and by 
doing so at camp a false impression is 
created in the minds of the campers. 
Applause is also out of place—the use 
of HOW! HOW! if satisfied and 
WAH! WAH! if not, will suffice. 

The ceremonial council ring was 
regarded in much the same light as we 
regard the sanctity of the church. No 
boisterdusness is allowed. The members 
of the tribe enter in single file behind 
the guide or leader. Silence on the 
part of the tribe is the custom. After 
the ceremony the tribe leaves silently 
and in single file. The council ring is 
never crossed. Only the firekeeper and 
those taking part in the ceremony are 
permitted in the ring. 

Suggested Ceremony 

The following ceremony as outlined 
is merely an example of the basic 
routines that may be used: 

1. All braves, led by a guide,' enter the 
ceremonial grounds in a clockwise 
direction to the steady beat of the 
drum. All remain standing. (Burn¬ 
ing torches placed at strategic in¬ 
tervals provide light along the trail 
and in the council ring.) 


2. Chief enters with two guides (Toe 
Heel Dance Step) and when seated 
bids others to be seated. '• 

3. Fire Dance. 

4. Headdress, bearer brings headress 
into the council ring and purifies it 
over the fire. He then places the 
headdress on the head of the kneel¬ 
ing chief. 

5. Peace pipe bearer enters and pre- 
• sents pipe to Medicine Man. 

6. Medicine Man approaches fire and 
lights pipe from the coals or burn¬ 
ing stick. 

7. The Medicine Man then proceeds 
with the PIPE CEREMONY: .., 

(a) kneeling (puffs pipe) blows 
smoke over the ground and says 
“to MUCK - A - EENA mother 
earth. May she bring us food”. 
(All spelling will be according to 
pronunciation). 

(b) Standing (puffs pipe) blows 

smoke to the sky and says “To 
WAKONDA the Great Spirit. May 
he smile upon us at this our council 
fire”. ... 

(c) Approaches the four winds, 
puffs on the pipe and bldws smoke 
in the direction of the, wind. (Note: 
Medicine Man may do any of the 
dance steps to move from the one 
wind to another.) 

North: “To O-K-GA the north 
wind. May he not come upon us 
with his cold and snow.” 

West: “To WA-TAY-GA the sun¬ 
set wind. May he bring us the rains 


158 


Canadian Camping 



that our crops may grow and we 
will have plenty.” 

South: “To WAZ-E-ATA the hot 
wind that he come not upon us 
with his great heat and dry up our 
lands and our water.” 

East: “To WAY-YO-HIN-YUN- 
PATA the sunrise wind. May it 
bring us the warm weather so that, 
with the help of the west wind, our 
. crops will grow.” 

8. Pow-wow Dance: Each dancer 
leaps into the air and proceeds to 
dance to the beat of the drum, using 
w hatever dance step he wishes. 

9. Chief goes to Medicine Man and 
receives the magic potion saying, 
“Oh give me of thy magic potion 
that I may rule the tribe of Camp 
— — — with great wisdom and 
courage. (Returns to place). 

10. Introduction of visitors. 

11. Dance. 

12. Awards. 

13. Dance. 

14. Story. 

15. Closing cermony — All chant the 
Omaha Tribal Prayer. 

At the conclusion of the prayer the 
chief closes the council using Indian 
sign language and saying: 

MAY THE GREAT SPIRIT — 
(right hand imitates smoke curling 
to the sky) 

MAKE—(hands move as in knead¬ 
ing putty) 

THE SUN RISE — (Chief touches 
left shoulder and then arches hand 
upwards and towards the members 
of the tribe, imitating the sun 
rising) 

IN YOUR — (points to others 
present) 

HEART — (Chief points to heart) 
WITH THIS OUR COUNCIL — 
(Large circle clockwise with right 


hand designating all who are 
present) 

IS ENDED — (Left hand paral¬ 
lel to the ground, right hand moves 
under.) 

16. All file out. 

The council fire may be lighted in 
several ways. The following will sum¬ 
marize various methods and materials 
used as published by numerous books 
and articles over the past years. 

Fire by friction is the most authentic 
method that can be used at a council 
ring ceremony. A fire by friction kit 
may be obtained from the local Boy 
Scout Association. 

The use of flint and steel is a little 
more difficult and should be used only 
when success can be guaranteed. 

In addition to these “on the spot” 
fire lighting methods, a runner with a 
flaming torch or flaming arrow may 
be utilized. The first two ways will 
require a special skill on the part of 
members of the tribe. For the sake of 
drama and time saving it is well to 
have the fire well laid so that the appli¬ 
cation of a single spark or flame will 
cause the whole to blaze. Many a 
ceremony has gotten off to a bad start 
because the Great Spirit failed to smile 
upon the fire lighter. 

Other ways, not authentic but effec¬ 
tive, are the use of chemical fires: Mix 
equal parts of granulated sugar and 
potassium chlorate in a cardboard box, 
surround with inflammable material 
and build the log fire around it. Over 
the box is balanced a small bottle con¬ 
taining about one (1) tablespoon of 
concentrated Sulphuric acid. Extreme 
care should be exercised in handling 
this material. From the bottle runs a 
string which is controlled by someone 
within the council ring. At the proper 
time the string is pulled tripping the 
acid into the chemicals, starting the 
fire in a startling and mysterious 
manner.

voluntarily or if asked to do so, is 
something for the director to consider.

There should be no attempt to cause 
tear or panic, since these diseases are 
rare, but they should be considered in 
planning camp health and safety pro¬ 
grammes. In the event that a camper 
develops unusual fever of unknown 
origin, it is important to supply the 
doctor with a detailed history. 

The Iollowing are suggestions about 
camp practices in relation to animal 
diseases:

wild animals, other than by watch¬

tice to leave nature alone as much 
as possible. 

2) Wild animals should not be cap¬ 
tured and kept alive, either on 
land or in the water. 

3) Birds, dead or alive, are best left 
alone, and birds nests should be 
sprayed by insecticide before being 
touched. 

4) The skinning of animals should 
be done only after spraying and 
putting on gloves. Careful wash¬ 
ing of the hands should follow. 

5) Local authorities should be con¬ 
sulted through the camp doctor 
about the presence of animal or 
insect diseases in that district. 

Finally, good health and safety 
practices in camping should include the 
repetition of the fundamentals of 
known methods of prevention. Staff 
and camper training should repeatedly 
be stressed. An awareness of potential 
hazards and a day-to-day practice of 
good healthy living should become a 
part of the daily pattern ol living. The 
camp director shoidd try to keep 
abreast of new developments in the 
health field through his own doctor. 
Much helpful literature can be ob¬ 
tained from the Department of Health, 
The Health League of Canada, The 
Department of Agriculture, and 
through such publications as “Today’s 
Health” published by the American 
Medical Association. Studies are going 
on by research workers in this country 
and elsewhere and gradually our know¬ 
ledge of the diseases which attack 
campers is increasing. It is hoped and 
expected that gradually methods will 
be found of preventing such diseases.

BANFF, ALBERTA TO HOST 

CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION CONFERENCE 
JANUARY 23 - 26, 1963 


At the annual meeting of the Canadian Camping Association in Montreal 
on March 22nd, Alberta s offer to host the next annual conference was accepted. 
It will be held in Banff at the Banff School of Fine Arts and Centre for Con¬ 
tinuing Education from January 23rd to 26th, 1963. The annual Camp Director’s 
Seminar of the Alberta Camping Association will form part of the Conference 
proceedings. 

The Banff School offers a unique and stimulating combination of education 
and recreation, in a setting conducive to both. Located seventy-five miles west 
of Calgary, it is easily reached by car, bus or train. T.C.A. Air Lines schedule 
several daily flights from east and west to Calgary where transportation by 
C.P.R., Greyhound Bus Lines or Hertz Car Rental is available. Those wishing 
to travel by car from eastern Canada may do so on the Trans Canada Highway 
or by alternate routes through the northern United States. 

The campus is beautifully situated on Tunnel Mountain, overlooking the 
town of Banff, the Bow River Valley and the Massive and Fairhohne Mountain 
ranges. The School is only a few minutes walk from downtown Banff and within 
easy walking distance of many points of interest such as the Hot Sulphur Swim¬ 
ming Pools, the Luxton Museum, the Banff Parks Administration Building, etc. 

The famous Mount Norquay Chair Lift and the Norquay ski slopes are but 
a half-hour’s drive from the School. The Sulphur Mountain Gondola Lift is 
even closer and provides a breath-taking view of the entire Banff area. The 
Lake Louise Sedan Lift is the longest of its kind in the world and offers a 
panoramic view of Assiniboinc to the south, Balfour to the west and beautiful 
Lake Louise in the foreground. 

The School’s facilities include a first-class dining room capable of catering 
to six hundred persons at a sitting, a Snack Bar, comfortable sleeping accommo¬ 
dation in well-appointed twin bedrooms, with or without bath, and spacious 
bright classrooms. A fireproof auditorium provides seating for six hundred 
persons. The Solarium and some of the larger classrooms and studios accommo¬ 
date up to two hundred. Exhibitions of paintings and other items are always on 
display, adding to the beauty and attractiveness of the setting. 

The on-campus chalets, with from twenty to thirty bedrooms each, have 
large picture windows offering an unexcelled view of the magnificent Bow Valley 
and attractive lounges with fireplaces, pianos, etc. Additional accommodation 
can be reserved by the School in downtown hotels, tourist cabins, and private 
homes as required. Twenty-five conference rooms and ten lounges are available 
for the Canadian Camping Association Conference. 

For additional information write directly to the Conference Chairman Mr 
Jack Alexander, 407-42nd S.W., Calgary, Alberta. 


162 


Canadian Camping 



RABIES 

Rabies is still with us and poses an ever present hazard to our 
campers this summer. It would be wise to warn campers against handl¬ 
ing ANY wild creatures this summer, whether they are alive or dead. 
This includes even mice, chipmunks, squirrels, rabbits—all animals. 

Campers should be urged to report immediately any bite or scratch 
from any animal. They should also report any wild creatures that 
appear to be acting in any manner that might be called — not normal. 
Notify the local M.O.H. or the Department of Lands and Forests at 
once. 

In addition to hospitalization there are usually medical expenses 
involved. These are not covered by the Ontario Hospital Insurance 
beyond the 24 hour emergency treatment prescribed under the Act. It 
is possible to buy an insurance plan from a private company to cover 
these medical expenses. Be sure to check the medical plan in your own 
province. 


AN HISTORIC OCCASION 

The evening of March 24th. 1962 was an historic evening, for at the closing 
banquet of the Ontario Camping Association’s Annual Conference, the first 
Taylor Statten Memorial Lecture was delivered by Professor Charles Hendry, 
Director of the School of Social Work at the University of Toronto. 

The Great Hall at Hart House was a perfect setting, with a warming fire 
burning that fenced with the shadows in the darkened room. 

Mr. Joseph McCully, Warden of Hart House, representing the Taylor 
Statten Memorial Fund was host for the lecture. Dr. Roger Myers introduced 
the speaker brilliantly and humorously and Ron Perry thanked Professor Hendry 
in his own inimitable style. 

Professor Hendry’s lecture was entitled “TOWARDS A NEW UNDER¬ 
STANDING OF LEADERSHIP”. He drew upon his experiences with the late 
Taylor Statten during the founding years of Camp Ahmek to illustrate his 
subject. The complete text of this lecture will be published by the Fund Com¬ 
mittee and made available to Canadian Camping members early in the fall. 

Mrs. Taylor Statten (Tonakela) was presented with an honoraiy life 
membership in the Ontario Camping Association, which was accepted in her 
absence by her daughter, Mrs. H. Ebbs. 

It was an inspiring and memorable evening. The greatest tribute to Taylor 
Statten was obvious but unstated. It lay in the caliber of the four Ahmek alumni 
at the head table, Professor Hendry, Dr. Myers, Ron Perry and Joseph McCully. 


Toronto , Canada , June 1962
