/. ALEX EDM ISON 

The Taylor Statten Memorial Fund has been established at the University 
of Toronto through the contributions of 400 men and women living in many 
parts of Canada and the United States who have so far contributed over $20,000. 

The purpose of the Taylor Statten Memorial Fund is to encourage the 
discovery and training of talented young people for professional careers in 
youth-serving occupations. Three types of grants are contemplated. Initially 
these will be made to assist qualified and worthy students intending to prepare 
themselves for one of the human service professions. Particular consideration will 
be given where work with youth in such settings as community agencies, religious 
institutions, organized camps and related programmes, is involved. 

As the Fund grows, two other types of grants will be possible: (1) Lecture¬ 
ships aimed at bringing to the University persons of outstanding achievement 
in the area of human growth and development and the youth services field, to 
give one or more public lectures and to serve as consultants to appropriate youth 
serving groups; and (2) Research grants to graduate students or to teaching staff 
when the research involved is concerned directly with problems of human growth 
and development. 

All grants will be made without respect to race, religion or nationality of 
the recipient. 

Since the first grant is being made in 1962, it is appropriate that tribute 
should be paid to Taylor Statten for whom this Fund constitutes in part a living 
memorial. 

Taylor Statten, who died on 1st November 1956 in Algonquin Park, Ontario, 
had a career in youth work and camping possibly without parallel in Canada. 
Like his artist friend, Tom Thomson, he passed away at storied Canoe Lake. 

Near him, in his Little Wapomeo Island cabin, was the large stone fireplace 
which Thomson had helped build so many years before. It bears this inscription: 

“There let the Northwoods Spirit 
Kindle Fires of Friendship.” 

The “fires” which Taylor Statten, or The Chief, as he was called by many 
thousands, himself kindled w'ere many and varied. There were those of friend¬ 
ship, most certainly. There were also those of inspiration to youth, the full 
dramatic effect of which must await a future time for proper evaluation. 

Taylor Statten, a native of Erindale, Ontario, became Boys’ Work Secretary 
at Central YMCA in Toronto in 1905. His long “Y” career included postings as 
Provincial, and then Canadian, Boys’ Work Secretary. In 1921 he was appointed 
Secretary to the National Boys’ Work Board. In 1914 he originated and, with a 
group of other interested persons, set up the Canadian Standard Efficiency 
Training Programme for Tuxis Boys and Trail Rangers. He left his imprint on 
the careers of countless Canadians when these projects gained popularity 
throughout the country. 


164 


Canadian Camping 



“Canada’s Mr. Camper” was the fitting designation given Taylor Statten. 
He was responsible for at least fifty-two camps conducted by the YMCA, the 
first being at Lake Couchiching in 1905. In 1920, he conducted a leadership 
training course at Canoe Lake and there in the following year he inaugurated 
Camp Ahmek for boys. This private camp soon established standards of camping 
which attracted outstanding leaders, among them Ernest Thompson Seton, the 
naturalist, and Jack Miner, the bird-life expert. Ahmek’s reputation became 
widespread. It continues now under the direction of Taylor Statten’s sons, Dr. 
Taylor Statten Jr. of Montreal and Dr. Page Statten of Toronto. 

In 1924 a girls’ camp, Wapomeo, was also established on Canoe Lake by 
Mr. and Mrs. Taylor Statten, despite warnings that co-educational camping 
would surely ruin Ahmek. Both, however, prospered under skilled cooperative 
management with a programme controlled to the needs of various aged boys and 
girls. The camp alumni has now reached considerable proportions and the third 
generation of Statten campers has started to enrol. The family tradition has 
continued at Wapomeo, too, with the Statten daughter, Adele (Mrs. J. H. Ebbs), 
in an active directional role. Taylor Statten was the first President of the 
Canadian Camping Association and the only Canadian to be elected President 
of the American Camping Association. His international camping influence will 
live on also in distant India, where in 1938 he established Camp Tonakela, near 
Madras, for underprivileged children. 

Whenever and wherever old friends and associates of Taylor Statten meet, 
they reminisce about his magnetism and inspirational qualities. The testimonials 
to his memory are many and warm and varied. Few speakers had such power 
over youth audiences. He had qualities of head and heart which were unforget¬ 
table. It would be difficult to estimate the number of young people he inspired 
to enter “Y” work, the ministry, the teaching profession, physical education, and 
other fields where leadership qualities are indispensable. What was his success 
secret? Many people could provide many answers. Most would probably make 
mention of his genuine interest in people, his gifts of understanding, his broad 
tolerance, his flair for friendship, and his intense love of Nature and all its attri¬ 
butes. His influences live on in many important quarters. It will continue in 
The Taylor Statten Memorial Fund . . . 

“far down the Future’s Broadening Way.” 


The general procedure regarding the fellowships is that applications should 
be forwarded to the Registrar of the University of Toronto, whose office will be 
available to give all preliminary information. The actual selection of the Taylor 
Statten Fellow for any given year will be made by the Taylor Statten Memorial 
Fund Committee. Lectures, such as the first Taylor Statten Memorial Lecture, 
will be arranged by the same Committee.

effective by the strength of the 
downward pressure of the hand on 
shaft, opposed to the outward push 
exerted by hand on grip. 

Indian Stroke: (two varieties) 

a. As in “J” stroke—recovery effect¬ 
ed by sliding the blade forward 
through the water, from the posi¬ 
tion at the end of “J”. This is 
done by bending forward the wrist 
of the hand on shaft, then sliding 
blade forward starting position is 
gained by bending wrist sharply 
back. Paddle does not revolve in 
hands. 

b. As in “J” stroke but at the mo¬ 
ment recovery begins, change the 
position of hand on grip to the 
other side of the grip, all the time 
holding the position firmly (no 
change) with hand on shaft. Re¬ 
cover paddle by sliding blade for¬ 


ward through water as before but 
resume starting position by twist¬ 
ing forward wrist of hand on grip 
and allowing shaft to turn in the 
other hand. Paddle revolves. 

Reverse “J” 

All action as the normal “J” stroke 
but direction is reversed (not sitting 
position). 

Figure of eight 

Two joined circles, paddled in a con¬ 
tinuous line, one with the paddle on 
the inside, the other on the outside. 
The inside circle to be accomplished 
by using one or more bow draws or 
strokes similar type and the outside 
circle by using one or more sweep 
stroke. Forward motion is to be 
maintained at all times. The paddle 
does not change sides during the per¬ 
formance of cne figure of eight.

At camp is there anyone who does 
not look up to the stars on a clear 
evening? In summer they seem to 
shine with a warm and friendly 
twinkle as compared to the chilly glit¬ 
ter of a frosty winter night. Yet they 
are always remote and mysterious, and 
for that reason fascinating to young 
and old who seek a little more knowl¬ 
edge. Let us see to it that our campers 
experience the thrill of star gazing in 
the camp setting, sensing at the same 
time the peace and beauty of the 
earth’s lakes, mountains and forests. 


In summer, especially if we are on 
daylight saving time, darkness comes 
too late for younger children, unless 
they can sleep in next morning. In 
July, the Constellations do not show 
clearly until almost 9.30. If campers 
are ready for bed, in pyjamas, jackets 
and warm socks, they can be in bed 
soon after 10 o’clock. For the 12 year 
olds and up, this is not too late, 
occasionally. 

Before dark is a good time for talk¬ 
ing about the stars and planets, look¬ 
ing at charts to see the shape and posi¬ 
tion of a few constellations and stars. 
There will be lots of questions, many 
beyond the ken of the amateur guide, 
but a good Star Book, such as the 
Golden Nature Guides, will give a few 
facts and figures to answer: “How 
far? What is a light year? What 
makes Northern Lights? How do you 
know if it’s a star or a planet?” 

A telescope or binoculars add inter¬ 
est, but the naked eye can see far more 
stars than can be remembered in a 
few evenings. 

Binoculars do give a spectacular 
view of the moon, showing plainly the 
darkened portion. 

An open field, preferably on a hill, 
is an ideal place for seeing the stars, 
and lying on a blanket is comfortable, 
but not necessary for short sessions, if 
no one minds a slight “crick” in the 
neck! Using a flashlight in pointing 
out the constellations seems to help. A 
good start for beginners is finding the 
true North. The Great Bear or Dipper 
is large and plain to see, and following 
the “pointers”, there is Polaris, the 
North Star! It is not very bright, but 
alone. Follow from Polaris the upward 
handle of the Little Dipper, or tail of 
the Small Bear—Vega, in Lyra, the

brightest star in the summer, is directly 
overhead, and below to the East is the 
Northern Gross or Swan, to the South 
is the triangle of Acquila the Eagle 
with its bright star. Altair. 

In the South the planets Saturn and 
Jupiter shine with steady brilliance, 
and towards the south-west, Antares a 
red star in Scorpius, is near the hori¬ 
zon. In the west, Arcturus, at the base 
of the kite shaped constellation, Bootes 
the Herdsman, is very bright. 

That is enough for one evening! The 
time goes all too quickly, but it is 
always good to end a program when 
campers are clamoring for more. The 
star gazers go quietly down the hill to 
bed. murmuring star names and quite 
probably dreaming of them later. 

When clouds spoil a star evening, 
have an indoor project, such as making 
a large circular black chart with the 
constellations traced in small silver 
stars the sticker kind. Star boxes are 
simple to make for younger campers— 
directions are found in Nature or Star 
books. 

Legends of the stars from ancient 
peoples of other lands, as well as our 
own North American Indians, can he 
told around campfires. Away from 
camp, on the shores of remote peaceful 
lakes, with the wide canopy of sky and 
stars overhead, there should he a star- 
wise member of every canoe trip party. 

The stars guided the earliest travel¬ 
lers by land, and navigators on the 
seas, and showed the way to flyers be¬ 
fore the invention of intricate instru¬ 
ments. Now in this dawning of the age 
of space discovery^, the stars and 
planets seem to have a more thrilling 
message. Let us help our campers to 
read what is written in the summer 
sky.

from page 159 

A snake fire is made by laying a 
magnesium ribbon in a spiral or other 
pattern, ending at the fire. Lit from 
the outside, its effect is quite startling. 
Caution: be sure it enters the council 
ring at a place where no one will be 
burned. In the construction of all fires 
it is better to experiment once or twice 
rather than miscue at the critical time. 

Coloured fires, although not authen¬ 
tic to the American Indian, may be 
utilized to add variety to the council 
fire programme. The following fires 
are suggested: 

White Fire 


Potassium Nitrate ...60 parts 

Sulphur Sublimate .20 parts 

Antimony Nigrum .10 parts 

Meal Powder . 6 parts 

Camphor Powder. 4 parts 


Method: Powder the camphor with 
the aid of a few drops of alcohol. The 
other ingredients must all be powdered 
separately and mixed together on a 
paper, not in a mortar. Any meal pow¬ 
der will do, but corn meal is the best. 
The addition of a little lycepedum will 
make the fire burn more uniformly. 


Potassium Nitrate .16 oz. 

Meal Powder . 4oz. 

Sulphur Sublimate . 8 oz. 

(all finely powdered) 

Red Fire 

Strontium Nitrate .40 oz. 

Potassium Nitrate .12oz. 

Shellac (finely powdered).12 oz. 


Method: Mix thoroughly on paper, 
not in a mortar. Be sure to have the 
shellac very finely powdered before 
mixing with other ingredients. 

Blue Fire 


Shellac pulverized . 3 oz. 

Alum Exsiccated . 1 yi oz. 

Sulphur Sublimated .. 1 /z oz. 


Method: Must all be powdered separ¬ 
ately first and then mixed together on 
a paper. 


Green Fire 


*Barium Nitrate .16 oz. 

^Sulphur Sublimate . 6 oz. 

*—mix these two together) 

**Potassium Chlorate . 4 oz. 

**Lainp Black . 1 oz. 

(**—mix these two together) 


Then finally mix the mixtures on paper 
with a spatula, NOT in a mortar. 

Yellow Fire 

Simply add a little salt (sprinkled 
on the flames) until desired effect 
is obtained. Too much salt will 
extinguish the fire. 

Chemical fires can add much to your 
pageant. However, you must realize 
that while it is fun to play with differ¬ 
ent coloured fires, it is also dangerous 
and there is no excuse for carelessness. 

VIGIL OR NAMING CEREMONY 

When a youth reached the age of 
manhood (13-15 years) he was sent 
out to prove himself by surviving in 
the woods without food or water for 
a certain length of time. He was given 
three marked arrows that were not to 
be used under any circumstances. Dur¬ 
ing the vigil the brave was required to 
commune with nature and have a med¬ 
icine dream. Upon the completion of 
the dream the brave would return to 
the tribe, telling the Medicine Man 
and the elders of his experience. From 
this he would receive his name and a 
medicine pouch or an eagle feather. 

This same ceremony, with slight 
variation, can be used as part of the 
camp Indian Lore programme. 

First of all the Vigil Ceremony must 
be considered as the highest honour 
attainable and is limited to Senior 
Campers and staff. A committee of 
three senior staff people is set up to 
screen all applicants who believe that 
they have reached the age of manhood. 

Upon acceptance of the written ap¬ 
plication stating the reason why the 
youth wants to participate in the vigil 
the brave is taken, before supper, by 
the Director to a secluded area and

told in which general direction he must 
set up camp and spend the night. At 
this time lie has a serious discussion 
with the Director concerning the Vigil 
and its significance to the applicant. 
This can be related to Christ’s trip into 
the wilderness in preparation for think¬ 
ing and communing with God. The 
applicant is given three marked mat¬ 
ches and allowed to use one, the rest 
to be returned the next morning before 
breakfast. During the ceremony the 
brave is without food or water from 
noon until breakfast the next day. 

Upon returning to camp the next 
morning the applicant relates his ex¬ 
perience to the committee. Any per¬ 
sonal decisions arc kept secret or di¬ 
vulged to the committee, as the person 
so wishes. Many participants gain a 
new insight into themselves and for 
some it is the first introduction to quiet 
meditation and prayer. 

The successful applicant, and it 
should be noted that simply because a 
person goes on a vigil does not neces¬ 
sarily mean that they will be accepted 
into the vigil order, is presented with a 
medicine pouch or eagle feather and 
given an Indian name related to his 
personality at the closing ceremonial. 
Criteria of a successful applicant 
should be in keeping with philosophy 
of the individual camp. 

Great care should be taken in the 
administration and handling of this 
programme. It should not be attemp¬ 
ted until an authentic Indian Lore pro¬ 
gramme has been established.

A Report On What U.B.C. Is Doing In Recreation . . . . 
Particularly Camp Leadership. 


OUTDOOR EDUCATION 


The University of British Columbia 
has in recent years been actively inter¬ 
ested in Outdoor Education, especially 
as it pertains to a greater and more 
effective use of the natural resources of 
the province. This interest started 
when President N. A. M. MacKenzie 
and Dean Geoffrey Andrew, Deputy 
President, set up an inter-faculty com¬ 
mittee to study ways that the univer¬ 
sity could give leadership in the broad 
area of Outdoor Education. 

As a result, a professional major in 
Recreation was added to the B.P.E. 
programme offered by the School of 
Physical Education. At the same time 
the name of the school was changed 
to the School of Physical Education 
and Recreation. In addition to this, 
another inter-faculty committee is at 
present working on the problem of 
having students at the university make 
better use of the many and varied 
outdoor recreational resources of the 
province. British Columbia is especial¬ 
ly bountiful in its natural resources 
suitable for the recreational pursuits 
of man. Within an hour’s driving time 
from Greater Vancouver, where three- 
quarters of the population of the pro¬ 
vince resides, one can ski, mountain 
climb, fish, hike, sail, cruise, camp, gar¬ 
den, hunt, amidst all the beauties of 
nature. 

A few statistics may be of interest at 
this point. 

Fishing licenses issued in 1960-185,000 
Hunting licenses issued in 1960... 125,650 


LORNE E. BROWN 

Associate Professor , Faculty of Education, 
UBC. Chairman, President's Committee on 
Outdoor Education, Camping and 
Conservation. 


No. of ducks killed by hunters, 

1959 ....390,200 

No. of moose killed by hunters, 

1959 . 12,200 

No. of deer killed by hunters, 

1959 . 61,400 

Provincial Parks in B.C.163 parks, 

8,400,000 acres 

Nature Houses (3 now located in 
Provincial Parks) 

1960 visitations—37,000 persons 

There seems to be little doubt that 
the wise and constructive use of the 
many recreational resources of the 
province is necessary. It also seems 
logical that the university is a suitable 
place to start an educational pro¬ 
gramme which would have far-reach¬ 
ing effects, as many graduates leave 
to take up residence in various parts 
of B.C. 

Another specific programme being 
carried on is that of Gamp Leadership. 
There are approximately 100 organized 
summer camps in B.C. with an annual 
attendance of just over 25,000 persons. 
Although organizations operate camps 
for different reasons, there is the com¬ 
mon basis of taking people away from 
their usual place of abode and having 
them live in a more natural setting, in 
groups, with an older person as a coun¬ 
sellor or leader. The camping move¬ 
ment has grown up like “Topsy” with 


Toronto, Canada, Jane 1962 


171 






often not too much attention given to 
high standards of programme and 
leadership. The training of the per¬ 
sons who are placed in charge of young- 
people on a 24-hour basis assumes 
rather important proportions, if lasting 
benefit is to come to those taking part. 
Therefore, through co-operative ef¬ 
forts, steps are now being taken to pro¬ 
vide short conferences and workshops 
in the camp setting or on the university 
campus for camp staffs at all levels 
of responsibility. 

Annual week-end conferences have 
been held the last three years, two on 
the university campus and one at the 
U.B.G. Forestry Camp at Loon Lake 
about 20 miles from Vancouver. These 
have been planned and organized by 
the President’s Committee in co-opera¬ 
tion with the B.C. Camping Associa¬ 
tion, the Community Programmes 
Branch of the Department of Educa¬ 
tion and the Department of Extension. 
U.B.C. 

Attendance at the first two confer¬ 
ences was just under 100 persons each 
year, with directors, senior staff, coun¬ 
sellors and committee people taking 
part. The 1962 workshop, at present 
in the planning stages, expects to have 
about 200 camping people attend. 

The planning committees for all 
three conferences have been composed 
of representatives from the Church 
camps, YMCA’s, Jewish groups, Board 
of Parks and Recreation, members of 
the executive of the B.C. Camping 
Association, personnel from various

departments and faculties within the 
University, and the Director of the 
Community Programmes Branch. Fin¬ 
ancial assistance was obtained from the 
University and the Community Pro¬ 
grammes Branch. For the two confer¬ 
ences held on campus, living accom¬ 
modation and meals were provided at 
a nominal cost. 

To date, the conference programmes 
have been a balance between the 
philosophical concepts of camping, im¬ 
portance of mature leadership, camp 
management and the acquisition of 
outdoor skills. The 1962 workship is 
being planned to use the small group 
discussion technique, with keynote 
speakers, films and dramatizations 
being used to provide the material to 
spark off the discussions. This will be 
a new experiment for the committee 
and evaluation of it will not be pos¬ 
sible until after the workshop. The 
general reaction of those attending 
each year has been very favorable. 
Many camp organizations use these 
conferences as a pre-requisite to their 
own in-service training. Most of them 
subsidize the people attending by pay¬ 
ing part or all the registration fee. 

The I act that requests are made to 
have the conferences continue each 
year, may indicate they are filling a 
need. One thing that seems to be sig¬ 
nificant is the fact that “camp” people 
from many varied and diversified 
groups are coining together and shar¬ 
ing ideas and experiences. This alone 
would seem to make the idea well 
worthwhile. At any rate, an effort is 
being made to raise the quality of resi¬ 
dential camping in B.C. through 
mutual co-operation and experience of 
all concerned. It is sincerely hoped 
that the boys and girls and the adults 
who attend any one of the 100 camps 
in B.C. will have, as a result of these 
conferences, a better and more en¬ 
riching experience.
